templates.name: Addition/similarity: a further item of the same kind
Contrast: established view or appearance, then a finding that breaks it
Contrast: positive claim, then a limiting fact about the same subject
Cause/effect: condition, principle or evidence, then its consequence
Concession: grant, then the main claim resumes (but / Still)
Emphasis: stronger same-direction fact (content-contrast trap at hard)
Specification/restatement: exact content or plain rewording
Sequence/time: next step, earlier or later event, end of a long effort
Culmination, alternative and place (ultimately, alternatively, there)
Example: general claim, then one named instance

items.passage: Aviation historians rank the de Havilland Comet, which in 1952 became the first jet airliner to enter commercial service, among the most influential aircraft ever built. ______ the original model’s career was brief: in 1954, two Comets broke apart in midair, and the fleet was grounded. Still, the investigation into those disasters reshaped the way later jetliners were engineered and tested.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence makes the main claim: historians rank the Comet “among the most influential aircraft ever built.” The blank sentence grants a fact that seems to cut against that claim: “the original model’s career was brief,” since two Comets “broke apart in midair, and the fleet was grounded.” The next sentence returns to the main claim with “Still,” noting that the investigation “reshaped the way later jetliners were engineered and tested.” “Granted” fits, since it introduces a point the writer concedes before restating the main claim.

A.why_wrong: The brief career and the grounding are not an instance of the Comet’s influence; they cut against that claim, which is why the next sentence opens with “Still.”

B.why_wrong: The crashes are not a further point in support of the claim that the Comet was influential; they are a setback the writer concedes before turning back to that claim.

D.why_wrong: The Comet’s standing among historians did not cause the original model’s career to be brief; the brief career is a concession, not a consequence.

items.notes: Grant then turn on the 3.19 / f5959727 shape (claim, concession in the blank sentence, Still resumes), keyed Granted (live K1 keys lean on Of course). K1 has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/transitions.md section 5), so it is written as a strong band 6 and band_target is 6, not the 7 the plan asked for. No contrast decoy (contrast and concession exclude each other) and no In fact, Indeed or Actually. Trap: Moreover for a reader who takes the crash history as more detail about the plane's significance. Facts kept general: Comet 1 entered service 1952, two midair breakups in 1954 (Elba, Naples), fleet grounded; the inquiry's fatigue findings shaped later design. Transitions: no web check (WAVE.md, 2026-10-16); real subject described from general knowledge, no researcher named, no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: The honeybee, with its egg-laying queen, its thousands of sterile workers, and its communal wax combs, has shaped popular conceptions of bees. Among the roughly 20,000 described bee species, however, such elaborate colonies are exceptional. ______ an individual female constructs a nest by herself, provisioning each brood cell with pollen and nectar before sealing an egg inside and abandoning it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes the popular picture of bees: colonies with a queen and thousands of workers. The second sentence says that among bee species, “such elaborate colonies are exceptional.” The blank sentence then describes what usually happens instead: “an individual female constructs a nest by herself.” “More often” fits, since it introduces the case that occurs more frequently than the exceptional one just mentioned.

B.why_wrong: The solitary female does not qualify or cut against the claim that colonies are “exceptional”; she is the common case that makes colonies the exception.

C.why_wrong: The rarity of colonies is not the reason that a female nests by herself; solitary nesting is the more common pattern, not a result of the colonies being rare.

D.why_wrong: The solitary nest is not a separate point added to the claim about colonies; it is the usual case that the exceptional colonies are being set against.

items.notes: Frequency form of S1 (d3b7d7a3 band 7, 4b7a84b0 band 6): a popular picture, a sentence saying that picture is the exception, then the usual case keyed More often. Band 7 move: surface contrast with a non-adversative key (the lone female looks like a turn away from the honeybee picture, so That said pulls a reader who links the blank sentence to the first sentence rather than the second). Blank opens a sentence rather than following a semicolon, to avoid the '; ______ researchers found,' skeleton already used by five live More often items. Decoy set varied from the model's (for this reason, additionally, nevertheless). Real general fact (most of the roughly 20,000 bee species are solitary nesters). Transitions: no web check (WAVE.md, 2026-10-16); real subject described from general knowledge, no researcher named, no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: In Italo Calvino’s Invisible Cities (1972), Marco Polo entertains the emperor Kublai Khan with descriptions of fifty-five imaginary cities, from one elevated on stilts to another suspended over an abyss by ropes and chains. Each seems stranger and more remote than the last. ______ Polo acknowledges that every description has, in some way, concerned a single city: his native Venice.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The text describes Polo’s accounts of “fifty-five imaginary cities,” each of which “seems stranger and more remote than the last.” The blank sentence reveals what all of these accounts finally come down to: “every description has, in some way, concerned a single city: his native Venice.” “Ultimately” fits, since it introduces the final, underlying point behind the surface variety of the cities.

A.why_wrong: Polo’s admission is not one more city or one more detail added to the list; it reveals what the whole list has been about.

B.why_wrong: The cities’ seeming stranger and more remote is not the reason they are all about Venice; the admission recasts the descriptions rather than following from them.

C.why_wrong: The admission is not an instance of a city that seems “stranger and more remote than the last”; it is a statement about all of the cities at once.

items.notes: Culmination on the 3.4 / 6e0c60da shape (and 332e75bf, band 7) (a surface impression, then what in the end matters), here about a work of literature. Band 6 by plan. No adversative decoy, since the turn from strange, remote cities to Polo's own Venice would let However or Nevertheless read as acceptable; Finally and Eventually also left out. Real book: Baucis on stilts and Octavia hung over an abyss by ropes and chains; Polo's line 'Every time I describe a city I am saying something about Venice' paraphrased, not quoted. Transitions: no web check (WAVE.md, 2026-10-16); real subject described from general knowledge, no researcher named, no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Ethiopia, where arabica coffee originated, grows more of the crop than any other country in Africa. Its role in the international coffee trade is more modest than that ranking might suggest, however; ______ roughly half of each year’s harvest is consumed domestically, much of it prepared in elaborate household ceremonies that involve roasting, grinding, and brewing the beans.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The text says that Ethiopia’s “role in the international coffee trade is more modest than that ranking might suggest.” The clause after the blank gives a fact that strengthens this point: “roughly half of each year’s harvest is consumed domestically,” so a large share of the crop never enters international trade. “Indeed” fits, since it introduces information that reinforces the preceding claim.

A.why_wrong: Domestic use of half the harvest does not hold true in spite of Ethiopia’s modest role in the coffee trade; it helps explain that modest role.

C.why_wrong: The domestic consumption is not a separate point added alongside the claim about trade; it is the evidence that shows why Ethiopia’s role in trade is modest.

D.why_wrong: Ethiopians do not drink their coffee in order to keep the country’s role in trade modest; the clause supports the claim rather than describing a step taken toward a goal.

items.notes: Band-7 emphasis on the 'unrealized' variant (3.6 / 00e0170f maglev) with the semicolon placement of 3.10 / 47e238be: a claim that X is smaller than expected, then a stronger same-direction fact keyed indeed. Surface contrast: the clause after the blank holds its own turn (consumed domestically rather than exported), so nevertheless pulls a reader who reacts to the however and the change of subject. No consequently decoy (reverse causation could make it defensible); to that end as in 3.6. Real general facts: Ethiopia is Africa's largest coffee producer and drinks about half its crop. Transitions: no web check (WAVE.md, 2026-10-16); real subject described from general knowledge, no researcher named, no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: On the Galápagos Islands, blue-footed boobies, seabirds named for their brilliantly colored feet, lay their eggs directly on exposed ground, in a shallow depression often encircled by accumulated droppings. Red-footed boobies, ______ construct platforms of interwoven twigs high in mangroves and other shrubs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The text says that blue-footed boobies “lay their eggs directly on exposed ground,” in “a shallow depression.” The sentence with the blank describes a second species that does the opposite: red-footed boobies “construct platforms of interwoven twigs high in mangroves and other shrubs.” “By contrast” fits, since it introduces a second subject whose nesting habits differ from those of the first.

A.why_wrong: Red-footed boobies do not nest the way blue-footed boobies do; one lays its eggs on exposed ground, and the other builds platforms of twigs in shrubs.

C.why_wrong: Red-footed boobies are not an example of birds that lay their eggs on exposed ground; they are a contrasting case.

D.why_wrong: The blue-footed boobies’ ground nests do not cause red-footed boobies to nest in trees; the text simply compares the two species.

items.notes: Two subjects, one attribute (nest site), opposite values, with the connective as an interrupter after the second subject (2.6 / 11df9b99 position). The first species is introduced on its own, not as one of 'several species', so for example cannot be read as introducing an instance. Real natural history (blue-footed boobies nest on bare ground in a ring of guano; red-footed boobies build twig nests in mangroves and other shrubs). Transitions: no web check (WAVE.md, 2026-10-16); real subject described from general knowledge, no researcher named, no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: In the early 1960s, the BBC held a monopoly on British radio. Agreements with record companies and musicians’ unions also restricted how much recorded music it could broadcast. ______ Radio Caroline, transmitting from a ship anchored in international waters off the English coast, played pop records almost continuously.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence says that agreements “restricted how much recorded music” the BBC “could broadcast.” The blank sentence describes a station that did the opposite: Radio Caroline “played pop records almost continuously.” “In contrast” fits, since it introduces a second station whose programming differed sharply from the BBC’s.

A.why_wrong: Radio Caroline did not restrict recorded music the way the BBC did; it played pop records almost continuously.

B.why_wrong: The sentence about Radio Caroline does not restate the point about the BBC’s limits; it describes a different station with different programming.

C.why_wrong: Radio Caroline is not an example of the BBC’s monopoly or of its limits on recorded music; it is a station that worked outside them.

items.notes: Two subjects with opposite values, blank sentence-initial (2.18 / cf11282b position), history and media. No causal decoy: Caroline was founded in part because of the BBC's limits, so As a result or Accordingly could read as acceptable. Real history: BBC radio monopoly until 1973, needle-time agreements limiting recorded music, Radio Caroline from 1964 on a ship off the English coast. Transitions: no web check (WAVE.md, 2026-10-16); real subject described from general knowledge, no researcher named, no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: The Yucatán Peninsula has almost no surface rivers or lakes, so for the ancient Maya who lived there, cenotes—sinkholes that expose underground water—were an indispensable source of drinking water. ______ some cenotes held religious significance: archaeologists have recovered jade, gold, pottery, and human remains, apparently deposited as offerings, from the Sacred Cenote at Chichén Itzá.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence presents one role that cenotes played for the ancient Maya: they “were an indispensable source of drinking water.” The blank sentence adds a second, separate role: “some cenotes held religious significance,” as the offerings recovered from the Sacred Cenote show. “Additionally” fits, since it introduces a further point about why cenotes mattered.

B.why_wrong: The religious role of some cenotes does not hold in spite of their use as a water source; the two roles do not conflict.

C.why_wrong: The religious role does not reword the claim that cenotes supplied drinking water; it is a new point.

D.why_wrong: The offerings at Chichén Itzá do not spell out how cenotes supplied drinking water; they show a different role.

items.notes: Two members of one list (two roles of the same thing) on the 2.11 / 39d1a519 and 2.10 / eea351c4 pattern. No similarity decoy (excluded beside an addition key) and no causal or contrast decoy: water's importance is one scholarly explanation of why cenotes were sacred, and practical against sacred could support By contrast. Real archaeology (Sacred Cenote dredged and dived from the 1900s; jade, gold, pottery and human remains recovered). Transitions: no web check (WAVE.md, 2026-10-16); real subject described from general knowledge, no researcher named, no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Biologists long hypothesized that pigeons bob their heads while walking in order to stabilize their visual field. In a 1978 experiment, a researcher in Canada tested this hypothesis. ______ he trained pigeons to walk on a treadmill, where their surroundings remained stationary relative to their eyes, and observed that the birds stopped bobbing.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence says that a researcher “tested this hypothesis.” The blank sentence explains exactly how the test was done: “he trained pigeons to walk on a treadmill, where their surroundings remained stationary relative to their eyes.” “Specifically” fits, since it introduces the precise details of the general statement that came before it.

A.why_wrong: Putting pigeons on a treadmill is not a result of the researcher’s testing the hypothesis; it is the test itself.

B.why_wrong: The treadmill experiment is not a second step taken in addition to testing the hypothesis; it is how the hypothesis was tested.

D.why_wrong: The treadmill experiment does not contrast with the statement that the researcher tested the idea; it describes that test.

items.notes: General statement, then its exact content (2.12 / 9e3a215b: investigated a relationship, then exactly which variables). No example decoy (example and specification exclude each other). Real experiment (1978 treadmill study of pigeon head-bobbing at a Canadian university), researcher left unnamed. Transitions: no web check (WAVE.md, 2026-10-16); real subject described from general knowledge, no researcher named, no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Glaciologists classify some glaciers, including many in Alaska, Svalbard, and the Karakoram mountains of Asia, as surge-type glaciers. ______ these glaciers alternate between long quiescent phases, often lasting decades, in which they barely move and brief episodes of dramatically accelerated flow. During a surge, a glacier can advance tens of meters in a single day.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence uses a technical term: some glaciers are classified “as surge-type glaciers.” The blank sentence explains in plain language what that term means: “these glaciers alternate between long quiescent phases” and “brief episodes of dramatically accelerated flow.” “That is” fits, since it introduces a clarification of the term just used.

A.why_wrong: The blank sentence does not say that the glaciers behave this way whatever their classification; it explains what the classification means.

B.why_wrong: The description of quiescent phases and surges is not a further fact added to the classification; it is what the classification means.

C.why_wrong: Glaciers do not alternate between quiescent phases and surges because glaciologists classify them as surge-type; they are classified that way because they behave like this.

items.notes: Restatement of a technical term in plain words (2.15 / 7c3f0145 defines cognate replacement; 3.1 unpacks a classification), blank sentence-initial rather than after an em dash as in 2.15. No specifically or for example on offer, since a definition can also read as specification. Real glaciology (surge-type glaciers cluster in Alaska-Yukon, Svalbard and the Karakoram; surges reach tens of meters a day). Transitions: no web check (WAVE.md, 2026-10-16); real subject described from general knowledge, no researcher named, no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: The common chiffchaff and the willow warbler, two small songbirds of European woodlands, are so alike in their olive-green plumage that even experienced birders struggle to tell them apart by sight. Their songs, ______ are unmistakable: the chiffchaff, as its name suggests, repeats two simple notes over and over.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says that the two birds look so alike that “even experienced birders struggle to tell them apart by sight.” The blank sentence says the opposite about their songs: they “are unmistakable.” “Though” fits, since it signals that this information about the songs contrasts with the difficulty of telling the birds apart by appearance.

B.why_wrong: The songs are not an example of the birds’ similar plumage or of birders’ trouble telling them apart; the songs are what make the birds easy to tell apart.

C.why_wrong: The birds’ similar plumage does not cause their songs to be unmistakable.

D.why_wrong: The songs are not alike in the way the plumage is; the two birds sing very different songs.

items.notes: Appearance, then the expert reality, with though as an interrupter after the subject (2.16 / f8c4591b shape; here the second subject is the songs rather than the experts). No other contrast word on offer (however or by contrast would also fit). Decoys varied from 2.16's (for example, in addition, therefore), and the second sentence describes one song rather than closing on an 'X does A, while Y does B' pair. Real natural history: chiffchaff and willow warbler are near-identical in plumage and told apart by song. Transitions: no web check (WAVE.md, 2026-10-16); real subject described from general knowledge, no researcher named, no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: California’s Mono Lake contains tufa towers, limestone columns that formed underwater where calcium-rich springs mixed with the lake’s alkaline water. In 1941, Los Angeles began diverting streams that fed the lake, and its level fell by about 14 meters over the following four decades. ______ dozens of towers now stand exposed along the shoreline, some rising several meters above the ground.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The text explains that the tufa towers “formed underwater” and that, after Los Angeles began diverting streams that fed the lake, its level “fell by about 14 meters.” The blank sentence gives the result of this drop: “dozens of towers now stand exposed along the shoreline.” “Hence” fits, since it introduces a consequence of the preceding information.

A.why_wrong: The exposed towers are not a case similar to the falling lake level; they are a result of it.

B.why_wrong: The towers do not stand exposed in spite of the drop in the lake’s level; they stand exposed because of it.

D.why_wrong: That the towers stand exposed is not a rewording of the statement that the lake’s level fell; it is an effect of that drop.

items.notes: Condition, then its consequence keyed Hence (2.14 / 17e49403; 1.5 / 04ad68ca: a change removes a constraint, then the result). The first sentence's 'formed underwater' is the fact the consequence needs. Real: Los Angeles diversions of Mono Basin streams from 1941, lake down about 45 feet by 1982, tufa towers left standing above the water. Replaces a Spirit and Opportunity draft (textbook fame, and adjacent to the claimed RS item on Mars rover power). items.passage: In a 2006 referendum, Montenegrin voters approved independence for their small, mountainous Balkan republic, barely clearing the 55 percent threshold required for approval. ______ Montenegro had been politically united with neighboring Serbia for nearly ninety years, first within Yugoslavia and later, from 2003, in a loose confederation known simply as Serbia and Montenegro.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes an event in 2006: Montenegrin voters “approved independence.” The blank sentence describes an earlier period: Montenegro “had been politically united with neighboring Serbia for nearly ninety years.” “Previously” fits, since it signals that the information in the blank sentence comes before the event in the previous sentence.

A.why_wrong: Montenegro’s long union with Serbia is not similar to its vote for independence; it is the situation that the vote ended.

C.why_wrong: The 2006 vote did not cause Montenegro to have been joined with Serbia; the union came first.

D.why_wrong: The union with Serbia does not give the exact details of the 2006 referendum; it describes the period before it.

items.notes: Reverse chronology keyed Previously (2.2 / a819d8b6), carried by the past perfect and the dates. No However on offer: independence against a long union could support a contrast reading. Real history (May 2006 referendum, 55.5 percent yes against a 55 percent threshold; union with Serbia from 1918, state union from 2003). C.why_wrong: The employees’ sorting is not an instance of airlines failing to reunite suitcases with their owners; it describes the work done at the center.

items.passage: Russian matryoshka dolls, wooden figures that nest one inside another, are manufactured from the inside out.
